deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. There are no formulas, numbers used in calculation, or derivations. It is a page of German notes on ancient Greek history, probably lecture or reading notes. It continues the previous page (Macedonian kings after Alexander, the Gallic invasion, Antigonus Gonatas). The marginal heading is 'Entstehung des Achäischen u. Aetholischen Bundes' (origin of the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues). A second marginal note at the bottom reads 'Römer' (the Romans).

Content, paraphrased:
(1) During the reign of Antigonus (Gonatas), a great political change took place in Greece.
(2) Achaean League:
- The 12 Achaean cities once had an alliance, which dissolved after Alexander's death.
- In 281 four cities expelled their tyrants and renewed the league, and the other cities soon followed.
- Aratus freed his native city (Sicyon) and is to be regarded as the founder of the league.
- Its guiding principle was complete political freedom.
- The allies met twice a year and sent envoys to Aegium.
- Its great men included Aratus (praised for love of liberty and integrity), Philopoemen and Lycortas. The '183' beside them is evidently Philopoemen's death year, 183 BC.
(3) Aetolian League:
- It was founded at about the same time.
- It had a council ('Geheimenrath', probably the apokletoi) and a general (strategos), and assembled yearly.
- It was less politically skilful than the Achaean League and became a plaything of other peoples.

The only numbers are BC dates (281, 183) and counts (12 cities, 4 cities, twice a year). Nothing is computed, so there is no mathematical problem to reconstruct.
errors: Historical simplification: Aratus (who freed Sicyon in 251 BC) was not strictly the founder of the Achaean League. The league was refounded in 281/280 BC by Dyme, Patrae, Tritaea and Pharae. Aratus was its most important later leader, so calling him 'Stifter' is loose but common in older textbooks.

The chronology in the surrounding pages follows older conventions. For example, Antigonus Gonatas' death is given as 243 on the neighbouring pages, whereas modern dating is 239 BC. This page itself contains no clear date error: 281 for the renewal of the league and 183 for Philopoemen's death are both standard.
The context suggests the notes may not be in Gauss's hand, or are lecture notes on history. Attribution to Gauss as author of the content is doubtful.

results.what: Historical notes on the founding and constitution of the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues (3rd century BC)
results.modern_name: Hellenistic federal leagues (koina) – textbook ancient history

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains no mathematics. It is a routine history note on Greek federal leagues, copied or summarised from standard sources. It has no bearing on Gauss's mathematical work.

checkable.asserts: Trivial chronology: about 30 years separate the refounding of the Achaean League (281 BC) from Aratus' liberation of Sicyon (251 BC). The latter date is supplied from standard history, not from the page.
Trivial: of the 12 Achaean cities, 4 renewed the league first, leaving 8 that followed later.

transcription_corrections: 'und mußte als Stifter' should probably read 'und muß als Stifter des Achaischen Bundes angesehen werden'. The image shows 'muß als' written together.
The marginal note at the bottom reads 'Römer'; this is correct and marks the transition to the Roman intervention.
'Geheimenrath' is a plausible reading of the image (the '[?]' can likely be dropped). It refers to the Aetolian council (apokletoi).
'183 Lycortas': the 183 is most likely the death year of Philopoemen (183 BC), after whom Lycortas led the league. It is not a date attached to Lycortas.
